The integral diverges to $+\infty$.

**Proof.**

Consider the integrand $f(t) = e^{t^2}$, which is even and strictly positive on all of $\mathbb{R}$.

It suffices to show that the half-line integral $\int_0^\infty e^{t^2}\,dt$ diverges, since by symmetry
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{t^2}\,dt = 2\int_0^{\infty} e^{t^2}\,dt.$$

For $t \geq 1$, we have $t^2 \geq t$, hence
$$e^{t^2} \geq e^{t} \quad \text{for all } t \geq 1.$$

Therefore
$$\int_0^{\infty} e^{t^2}\,dt \geq \int_1^{\infty} e^{t^2}\,dt \geq \int_1^{\infty} e^{t}\,dt = \lim_{R\to\infty}\bigl(e^{R} - e\bigr) = +\infty.$$

Since $e^{t^2} > 0$ everywhere, the integral is bounded below by a divergent integral, so
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{t^2}\,dt = +\infty.$$

The integral does not converge to a finite value.
